title: A labelled rig drawing links the hardware to the model: what stays, what is idealised
summary: A CAD view of a test rig is the bridge between the lab hardware and the simulation domain. Read it for the order of components along the flow path, then ask which parts the model keeps, which it replaces by a boundary condition and which it leaves out.

media.alt: SolidWorks-style rendering of a pipe rig: a vertical flanged section labelled preheating section rises and bends through ninety degrees into a long horizontal flanged pipe labelled combustor. A short lance enters at the bend, and a ceramic honeycomb is labelled just after it. Small holes are visible along the pipe.

read_the_figure.question: What is the physical path of the air and fuel through the rig, and which of its parts does the CFD model represent?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes and no scale. It is a CAD rendering with four red text labels and leader arrows: lance, ceramic honeycomb, preheating section (inside a green box) and combustor. Flow runs up the vertical section, round the bend and along the horizontal pipe.
look_at: The green box marks the preheating section: a vertical run of flanged pipe segments. Flanges and bolts show where the rig comes apart.
The lance enters at the top of the bend as a thin horizontal tube; the honeycomb sits a short distance after the bend, before the long combustor pipe.
The small round holes along the pipes are ports, presumably for probes or instruments; the image does not say what they are for.
Compare with the 3D geometry drawing: the same layout reduced to a smooth pipe with a bend, a lance and a honeycomb, with the preheater replaced by an inlet.
read_the_figure.proves: That the CFD geometry is derived from real hardware and in what order the parts sit. It does not prove that the model reproduces the rig; no measurement is shown.
if_wrong: A model that omits a part that matters, for example heat loss through the preheater walls, will give boundary temperatures that are too high.
A model that keeps every port and flange becomes unmeshable; one that removes the bend loses swirl and mixing.
A model whose inlet profile is assumed flat when a bend sits just upstream will see a wrong velocity distribution at the lance.
must_check: A scale or a dimension: this image has none, so the dimensions must come from the drawing figure.
Which hardware is inside the model domain and which is replaced by a boundary condition.
Where measurements were taken on the rig, since those locations are what a simulation could be compared with.
The flow direction is stated (here it can be inferred from the lance and the labels).
Materials of the flow path; the project text brings a 2400 K tuyere material limit into the discussion.

terms.meaning: Blowing finely ground coal into the hot blast of a blast furnace through a lance so that it burns in the tuyere zone.
The part of the rig where the air is brought to the blast temperature before it meets the fuel.
The long pipe where fuel and air burn and the flame can be observed or measured.
A block of narrow parallel channels that straightens the flow and can anchor or shield the flame.
Replacing real hardware by a simpler computational region plus boundary conditions.
The ratio of inertial to viscous forces, which tells whether the flow in a pipe is laminar or turbulent.
How long a fluid element spends in a section: length over mean speed.

remember: A CAD view orders the components along the flow; the simulation keeps only those that matter to the question.
Anything replaced by a boundary condition (such as the preheater) must be specified from measurement or from a separate calculation.
Re above about 4000 in a pipe means turbulent; below about 2300 laminar; in between is transitional.
Residence time sets how much chemistry can happen before the end of a section.
A drawing with no scale is a diagram, not a dimension source.

understand.title: From hardware to domain
understand.text: The rig has a vertical preheater, a bend, a lance, a honeycomb and a combustor. The CFD drawings keep the lance, bend and combustor and the honeycomb, and represent the preheater by an inlet condition. That is a deliberate trade of fidelity for a mesh that can be built and run.

understand.title: Why the honeycomb matters
understand.text: It sets the velocity profile that the flame or coal sees. It is also the part that makes meshing hard, which is why the project text records that the flame-anchoring study was dropped.

steps.title: Reynolds number in the combustor pipe
steps.note: For a pipe of diameter D. The drawing figure gives D = 60 mm; the flow speed and fluid properties are not in the figures, so the worked example uses illustrative values.

steps.title: Residence time in a section
steps.note: For the 1015 mm run printed in the drawing and a speed of 5 m/s this is about 0.2 s. The speed is an assumed illustration.

steps.title: Laminar pressure drop in one honeycomb channel
steps.note: Each channel is small enough that flow in it is laminar, and the Darcy friction factor is 64 over Re. The hydraulic diameter of a regular hexagon equals its width across flats, so D_h is about 5 mm for the printed cell size.

steps.title: Speed inside the channels
steps.note: The honeycomb blocks some of the area, so the channel speed is the pipe speed divided by the open-area fraction phi. With the printed 5 mm cell and 0.25 mm spacing phi is about 0.91 (see the geometry explainer).

worked.title: Is the flow in the combustor pipe turbulent, and in a honeycomb channel?
worked.problem: Use illustrative values: cold air, density 1.2 kg/m3, viscosity 1.81e-5 Pa s, mean speed 5 m/s in the 60 mm pipe, and an assumed honeycomb length of 50 mm. Find the pipe Reynolds number, the channel Reynolds number and the channel pressure drop.

solution.text: Channel speed with phi = 0.91, then channel Reynolds number with D_h = 5 mm.
Laminar friction and pressure drop over 50 mm.

worked.answer: The pipe flow is turbulent (about 20,000) and each honeycomb channel is laminar (about 1,800). The pressure drop across the honeycomb is a few pascals. All inputs except the printed 60 mm and 5 mm are illustrative; hot gas would change every property.

analyze.q: The preheating section is outside the CFD domain drawn in the other figures. List what must then be specified at the inlet of the domain and how you would obtain it.
analyze.hint: Velocity profile, temperature, composition and turbulence level.

analyze.q: The pipe flow is turbulent but the honeycomb channels are laminar in the worked example. What does that do to the turbulence just after the honeycomb?
analyze.hint: Think of the channels as removing eddies larger than their size.

analyze.q: Which components in the image would cause the largest differences between a 2D axisymmetric model and the real rig?

evaluate.q: From this image alone, can the simulation be validated against the rig? What would you need?
evaluate.hint: Measurement locations, instruments and operating conditions.

evaluate.q: The image has no scale bar. How should a figure like this be captioned so a reader is not misled?
evaluate.hint: Say where the dimensions are given.

create: Draw a block diagram of the rig in flow order with each block marked as modelled, replaced by a boundary condition, or omitted, and with one line explaining why.
Propose a measurement plan at three locations along the combustor that would let a simulation be compared with the rig, and name the instrument for each.

checks.q: What is the role of the honeycomb in this rig?
checks.hint: Think of velocity profile and swirl.
checks.answer: It straightens the flow and evens the velocity profile before the combustor, and it can influence where the flame sits.

checks.q: Air at 5 m/s in a 60 mm pipe (density 1.2, viscosity 1.81e-5). Is it laminar or turbulent?
checks.answer: Re is about 2.0e4, well above 4000, so turbulent.

checks.q: Why would a CFD model replace the preheating section by an inlet boundary condition?
checks.answer: The preheater is long and its detail does not affect the combustion question; an inlet profile at the right temperature and speed represents it at a fraction of the mesh cost, provided the profile is realistic.

checks.q: The CAD image shows small holes along the pipes. Should they be modelled?
checks.answer: Only if they matter to the flow or are open to the flow. Closed instrument ports are normally omitted; open ones would act as leaks or sampling points and might need modelling.

checks.q: How would you document which parts of the rig are in the model?
checks.answer: A table listing each hardware part, whether it is modelled, replaced by a boundary condition or omitted, and the reason, placed next to this figure.
